title: Martin D-21 History And Changes: 1955 To 1969
description: Martin D-21 production changes from the 1955 samples through 1969, including binding, saddles, neck reinforcement, bridge plates and rosewood.
lede: The original D-21 kept its spruce top, rosewood body and rosewood fingerboard and bridge throughout its short production run. The changes came in its fittings and construction: a shorter saddle in 1965, black trim and new neck reinforcement in 1967, rosewood bridge plates in 1968, and the back-and-side wood transition in 1969.

hero.alt: Full front of a 1961 Martin D-21 in its open case
hero.caption: 1961 Martin D-21 from the Joe's Vintage Guitars photo archive.

sections.heading: D-21 Changes By Year
sections.html:
Year Or PeriodWhat Changed
1955Martin built six D-21 samples, combining a rosewood dreadnought body with simpler Style 21 appointments.
1956The D-21 entered the regular line. It had a 14-fret neck, rosewood fingerboard and bridge, and tortoise-colored binding and pickguard.
1965The bridge changed from the long through-saddle pattern to a short drop-in saddle.
1967Black plastic replaced tortoise-colored binding and pickguards. Square steel tube neck reinforcement replaced the earlier steel T-bar during this period.
April 9, 1968Martin changed its steel-string bridge-plate material from maple to rosewood. This is a construction change separate from the body-wood change the following year.
1969Martin recorded D-21 serial 254498 as its first official East Indian rosewood guitar. The original D-21 run ended that year.

sections.heading: 1955 And 1956: A New Rosewood Dreadnought
sections.html:
Six samples preceded the D-21’s public introduction in 1956. Its body followed the 14-fret dreadnought pattern, with a spruce top and Brazilian rosewood back and sides. Style 21 supplied relatively plain decoration and rosewood for both the bridge and fingerboard.

Those fittings separated it from the contemporary D-28, which used ebony for its bridge and fingerboard. The D-21’s rosewood body also separated it from the mahogany-bodied D-18. These were original model specifications, rather than changes introduced partway through the D-21 run.

sections.heading: 1956 To 1964: The Original Neck And Bridge
sections.html:
Early D-21s had an unbound fingerboard with dot markers, a rosewood belly bridge with a long saddle, and tortoise-colored body binding and pickguard. The neck contained a nonadjustable steel T-bar. Under the bridge, the top was reinforced by a small maple bridge plate.

The 1961 D-21 pictured here belongs to this earlier period. Its dot-marked fingerboard and headstock photographs illustrate the model’s plain decoration; the photographs do not establish a separate specification change in 1961.

photos.alt: 1961 Martin D-21 headstock face and tuners
photos.caption: The headstock face of the same 1961 D-21.

photos.alt: Worn fingerboard near the nut of a 1961 Martin D-21
photos.caption: Wear in the first frets of the 1961 D-21's fingerboard.

sections.heading: 1965 To 1967: Saddle, Trim And Neck Changes
sections.html:
In 1965, Martin replaced the long through saddle with a shorter drop-in saddle. The bridge remained rosewood. Changing the saddle arrangement did not turn the D-21 into an ebony-bridge model.

The next visible change came in 1967, when black plastic replaced the earlier tortoise-colored binding and pickguards. Martin also moved from a steel T-bar to square steel tube neck reinforcement in 1967. Both neck systems were nonadjustable; this was not the introduction of an adjustable truss rod.

sections.heading: 1968 And 1969: Bridge Plates And Body Wood
sections.html:
The factory’s April 9, 1968 bridge-plate change replaced maple with rosewood. The bridge plate sits inside the top, beneath the bridge. Its material is independent of the rosewood used for the exterior bridge, fingerboard, back and sides.

In late 1969, the back-and-side wood changed as Martin moved away from standard Brazilian rosewood production. D-21 serial 254498 is the factory’s recorded first official East Indian rosewood guitar. That milestone belongs to an overlapping material transition, so it does not make every 1969 guitar the same wood species.

sections.heading: When Did The Original D-21 End?
sections.html: The original D-21 production run ended in 1969. Later guitars bearing D-21 names, including the D-21 Special, belong to later production programs and can have different specifications. The Martin serial-number guide dates the instrument separately from its model name.

sections.heading: Did The D-21 Change To An Ebony Fingerboard?
sections.html: Rosewood was the fingerboard and bridge specification of the original D-21. An ebony replacement on an individual guitar is a repair or modification, not evidence of a standard late-1960s D-21 specification change.

title: Martin D-35 And D-35S History And Changes
description: Follow Martin D-35 development from its 1965 introduction through 1969: three-piece backs, light bracing, the D-35S, bridge plates and rosewood.
lede: The D-35 arrived in 1965 with a three-piece rosewood back, a bound ebony fingerboard and lighter top braces than the D-28. Its early history includes small trim revisions, the 12-fret D-35S, and the late-1960s changes to neck reinforcement, bridge plates and rosewood.

hero.alt: Full front of a 1967 Martin D-35
hero.caption: 1967 Martin D-35, the 14-fret version. The D-35S discussed below has a different 12-fret layout.

sections.heading: Model Changes By Year
sections.html:
Year Or PeriodWhat Changed
1965The D-35 joined the line with a three-piece Brazilian rosewood back, bound ebony fingerboard and 1/4-inch top braces.
August 1966The fingerboard binding changed from mitered corners at its lower end to a simpler joint.
1966 To 1967Black pickguards replaced the earlier tortoise-pattern guards during this transition. In 1967, square steel tube neck reinforcement replaced the steel T-bar.
January 1968A batch of 25 D-35S guitars marked the expansion of the 12-fret version. Earlier special-order 12-fret D-35s preceded this batch.
April 9, 1968Martin’s steel-string bridge-plate specification changed from maple to rosewood.
Late 1969East Indian rosewood entered standard production as Brazilian rosewood supplies ran down. The three-piece back remained part of the D-35 design.

sections.heading: 1965: The Three-Piece Back And Lighter Bracing
sections.html:
The D-35’s three-piece back allowed Martin to use narrower pieces of Brazilian rosewood than a conventional two-piece dreadnought back required. A center wedge separated the outer panels. White fingerboard binding and extra back seams made the new model visibly different from the D-28.

Inside, the D-35 used 1/4-inch top braces instead of the D-28’s 5/16-inch braces. These early D-35 braces were not scalloped. Brace width and scalloping describe different features: the D-35 was lighter-braced without returning to the carved brace profiles of prewar dreadnoughts.

photos.alt: Three rosewood back sections on a 1967 Martin D-35
photos.caption: The three-piece back of the 1967 D-35.

sections.heading: 1966 And 1967: Binding, Pickguard And Neck Revisions
sections.html:
Early fingerboard binding had mitered corners where it turned across the end of the board. That detail changed in August 1966. The ebony board and its white binding remained part of the model.

During the 1966 to 1967 transition, black pickguards replaced the earlier tortoise-pattern material. Martin also changed its nonadjustable neck reinforcement from a steel T-bar to square steel tubing. The 1967 guitar in these photographs shows the three-piece back and bound fingerboard, both features present from the model’s introduction.

photos.alt: Close-up of the bound fingerboard on a 1967 Martin D-35
photos.caption: Fingerboard binding on the same 1967 D-35.

sections.heading: 1968: The D-35S Becomes A Regular Production Variant
sections.html:
The D-35S used a 12-fret body-and-neck layout, with the neck meeting the body at the twelfth fret rather than the fourteenth. Its longer upper body, slotted headstock and wider neck distinguished it from the standard D-35.

A batch of 25 D-35S guitars was made at the end of January 1968. Special-order 12-fret D-35s existed earlier, so 1968 describes the expansion into regular production rather than the first possible example. The S version retained the three-piece back and Style 35 decoration.

sections.heading: 1968 And 1969: Bridge Plates And Rosewood
sections.html:
Early D-35s used a small maple bridge plate. Martin’s factory history dates the steel-string change to rosewood plates to April 9, 1968. The later plate specification belongs to the same original D-35 production era as the earlier maple version.

The exterior wood changed in late 1969 as East Indian rosewood entered standard production. Brazilian and Indian rosewood overlap during the transition; a three-piece back does not identify the species. The D-35 continued beyond 1969 with its three-piece construction intact.

sections.heading: Did The D-35S Replace The D-35?
sections.html: No. The 12-fret D-35S joined the line alongside the standard 14-fret D-35. It offered a different body-and-neck layout while retaining the three-piece back and Style 35 appointments.

sections.heading: Did The First D-35 Have Scalloped Braces?
sections.html: No. The original D-35 used lighter 1/4-inch braces with a non-scalloped profile. The combination distinguishes it from both a contemporary D-28 and a prewar scalloped-brace dreadnought. Joe’s Martin construction guide explains the brace and neck changes shared across the period.

title: Martin D-28 And D-28S History And Year Changes
description: Martin D-28 development from 1931 through 1969, including the 14-fret body, brace position, neck width, scalloping, herringbone, bridge plates and rosewood.
lede: The D-28 changed substantially between its 1931 introduction and the end of the 1960s. Its history runs from a 12-fret dreadnought to the 14-fret model, then through changes in brace position, neck width, brace carving, top trim, bridge design and rosewood. These changes happened at different times.

hero.alt: Body front of a 1959 Martin D-28 in its case
hero.caption: 1959 Martin D-28. This 14-fret example differs from the 12-fret D-28S discussed below.

sections.heading: Model Changes By Year
sections.html:
Year Or PeriodWhat Changed
1931The first D-28s used a 12-fret body, spruce top, Brazilian rosewood back and sides, and herringbone top trim.
1934The 14-fret D-28 entered production. T-frets and steel T-bar neck reinforcement replaced the earlier bar-fret and ebony-reinforced construction during this period.
1938The X-brace intersection moved rearward, farther from the soundhole. The braces remained scalloped.
1939The standard 14-fret neck narrowed from a 1 3/4-inch nut to 1 11/16 inches.
Late 1944Scalloped bracing ended. Martin had built 1,451 D-28s before this change.
1945 And The Later 1940sTapered braces followed the scalloped pattern, then developed into the straighter postwar profile. During the 1945 to 1946 transition, Sitka spruce replaced red spruce as the usual top material.
1946 To 1947Herringbone top trim gave way to the simpler postwar border. The trim change came after the end of scalloped bracing.
1965The long through saddle gave way to a short drop-in saddle.
1967Black pickguards replaced tortoise-pattern guards. Square steel tube neck reinforcement replaced the steel T-bar.
December 1967 And 1968Regular D-28S production restored the 12-fret body pattern alongside the 14-fret D-28, following earlier 1960s special orders.
April 9, 1968Martin changed from maple to rosewood bridge plates.
Late 1969East Indian rosewood entered standard back-and-side production as Martin phased out standard Brazilian rosewood sets.

sections.heading: 1931 To 1934: From Twelve Frets To Fourteen
sections.html:
The first D-28 was a 12-fret dreadnought with a slotted headstock. In 1934, Martin introduced the 14-fret D-28, reshaping the upper body to give the player two more frets clear of the body. Brazilian rosewood, a spruce top, ebony fingerboard and bridge, and herringbone top purfling defined Style 28 in this period.

The 1934 construction changes also included T-shaped frets and steel T-bar neck reinforcement in place of bar frets and an ebony reinforcement strip. The new body pattern and new neck construction were separate changes, even though both belong to the same period.

sections.heading: 1938 And 1939: Bracing Position And Neck Width
sections.html:
In 1938, the X-brace intersection moved farther back from the soundhole. This changed where the top was supported, but Martin still scalloped the braces. Rear-shifted bracing and scalloped bracing therefore occur together on original late-1930s D-28s.

The standard 14-fret nut width narrowed in 1939, from 1 3/4 inches to 1 11/16 inches. The familiar early wide-neck, forward-braced combination gave way through two successive changes. The prewar Martin guide places these changes alongside other models of the period.

photos.alt: D-28 model stamp and serial number 224411 on a 1967 Martin neck block
photos.caption: A different D-28, from 1967: the neck block carries model D-28 and serial 224411.

sections.heading: 1942 To 1947: Wartime Necks, Brace Carving And Herringbone
sections.html:
Wartime material shortages interrupted the use of steel neck reinforcement. Ebony reinforcement appears in parts of the 1942 to 1946 production period, with overlap rather than a single uninterrupted substitution.

Scalloped braces ended in late 1944. Tapered braces followed, before the straighter postwar profile developed later in the decade. Martin’s recorded total before the end of scalloping was 1,451 D-28s.

Herringbone survived beyond the bracing change and disappeared during the 1946 to 1947 transition. A herringbone D-28 can therefore have original tapered, non-scalloped braces. During the 1945 to 1946 transition, Sitka spruce replaced red spruce as the usual top material. Individual transition guitars and later exceptions prevent a universal species rule based on year alone.

photos.alt: Interior maker stamp on a 1967 Martin D-28
photos.caption: The interior center strip of the same 1967 D-28, showing the maker's stamp and Made in U.S.A. wording.

sections.heading: The 1950s And 1960s: The Postwar D-28 And D-28S
sections.html:
The postwar D-28 retained a two-piece rosewood back, ebony fingerboard and bridge, and 14-fret neck. Its simpler top border and non-scalloped bracing distinguish it from the earlier herringbone era. The 1959 D-28 shown above belongs to this postwar form.

Earlier 1960s special orders preceded the regular D-28S batch in December 1967 and its place in the 1968 line. The D-28S restored a 12-fret dreadnought configuration alongside the 14-fret model. The late-1960s version combined a slotted headstock with a wider neck and longer upper body. The S suffix had also been used for special orders in earlier periods, so that later meaning should not be applied to every prewar S stamp.

sections.heading: 1965 To 1969: Saddles, Pickguards, Plates And Rosewood
sections.html:
The long through saddle changed to a short drop-in saddle in 1965. In 1967, black pickguards replaced tortoise-pattern guards, and square steel tube neck reinforcement replaced the T-bar. These were factory changes within the postwar D-28 design.

Maple bridge plates gave way to rosewood on April 9, 1968. The bridge plate is the interior reinforcement under the bridge; the exterior D-28 bridge remained ebony.

The back-and-side wood transition came in late 1969, when East Indian rosewood entered standard production. Brazilian rosewood continued into this transition, so a 1969 serial is not a species identification. The serial-number chart supplies the production year, while the guitar’s construction establishes its particular combination of features.

sections.heading: Did Scalloped Bracing End With Herringbone Trim?
sections.html: No. Scalloped bracing ended in late 1944; herringbone top trim continued into the 1946 to 1947 transition. The two features changed on different schedules.

sections.heading: Is The D-28S The Same As An Early D-28?
sections.html: The late-1960s D-28S returned to a 12-fret body-and-neck layout, but it used the construction of its own production period. It was not a complete return to the bar frets, neck reinforcement and scalloped bracing of the earliest D-28s.

title: Martin D-45 History And Changes Through 1969
description: Martin D-45 development from the 1933 Autry guitar through 1969: 14-fret bodies, 1939 hexagon inlays, the 1942 stop and the 1968 return.
lede: The D-45 has two distinct early production periods: the original guitars made from 1933 through 1942, and the model’s return in 1968. The first period includes the move from a custom 12-fret guitar to the 14-fret model and the 1939 change to hexagon inlays. The reintroduced D-45 used late-1960s construction.
facts: Pearl Borders On Top, Back And Sides

hero.alt: Full front of a sunburst 2005 Martin D-45 with pearl trim
hero.caption: 2005 Martin D-45, shown to illustrate the model's pearl-trimmed appearance. The guide below covers D-45s made through 1969.

sections.heading: D-45 Changes By Year
sections.html:
Year Or PeriodWhat Changed
1933The first D-45 was built for Gene Autry with a 12-fret neck and slotted headstock. Style 45 pearl decoration extended around the top, back and sides.
Mid-1930sCustom production expanded to include 14-fret D-45s alongside the early 12-fret design.
1938The D-45 entered the catalog after its earlier custom-order period. Rear-shifted bracing also appears during this period.
1939Hexagon fingerboard inlays became the standard D-45 pattern, replacing snowflakes. The standard 14-fret dreadnought nut width narrowed to 1 11/16 inches during this period.
1942The original D-45 run ended after a total of 91 guitars.
1968The D-45 returned with a 14-fret neck, hexagon inlays and non-scalloped bracing. Martin’s bridge-plate change from maple to rosewood is dated April 9, 1968.
1968 And 1969Roughly 230 Brazilian rosewood D-45s were made during the initial revival period.
Late 1969The revival reached Martin’s transition toward East Indian rosewood for standard production.

sections.heading: The 1930s: From Custom Orders To The Catalog
sections.html:
Gene Autry’s 1933 guitar established the D-45 as a pearl-trimmed dreadnought. It had a 12-fret neck and slotted headstock. The small custom-order period that followed included both 12-fret and 14-fret instruments. The D-45 became a cataloged model in 1938.

Style 45 carried pearl around the top, back and sides, with an ornamented fingerboard and headstock. The guitar still belonged to the rosewood dreadnought family: spruce top, Brazilian rosewood back and sides, and ebony fingerboard and bridge. Its decoration distinguished it from the plainer D-28.

sections.heading: 1938 And 1939: Bracing, Neck Width And Inlays
sections.html:
The late-1930s dreadnought changes reached the D-45 as well as the plainer models. The X-brace moved rearward in 1938, and the standard 14-fret neck narrowed from a 1 3/4-inch nut to 1 11/16 inches in 1939. The braces remained scalloped.

In 1939, hexagons became the standard fingerboard inlay pattern in place of the earlier snowflakes. Early custom instruments can depart from the standard sequence, so this date describes the production-pattern change rather than a claim that no hexagon example could precede it.

photos.alt: Pearl headstock lettering and gold tuners on a 2005 Martin D-45
photos.caption: Vertical pearl headstock lettering on the 2005 D-45. This later example illustrates ornament, not prewar hardware specifications.

sections.heading: 1942: The Original Run Ends
sections.html:
Martin stopped the original D-45 run in 1942. Total prewar production was 91 guitars. That number covers the original run, including the earliest custom instruments; it is not a count of every later guitar carrying a D-45 name.

There was no continuous D-45 production through the 1950s. Later pearl-trimmed conversions of other Martin models belong to their own repair and modification histories, not to the factory’s 91-guitar total.

sections.heading: 1968: The D-45 Returns With Postwar Construction
sections.html:
The D-45 returned in 1968 after more than two decades out of production. It combined Style 45 decoration and hexagon inlays with the then-current 14-fret dreadnought construction. The neck used square steel tube reinforcement, and the top had non-scalloped braces.

Martin dates the move from maple to rosewood bridge plates to April 9, 1968. The restored model therefore belongs to a bridge-plate transition year. A late-1960s D-45 is not a prewar structural specification reproduced solely because its model number and pearl trim match.

sections.heading: 1969: Brazilian Rosewood And The Material Transition
sections.html:
The first two years of the revival produced roughly 230 Brazilian rosewood D-45s. Published counts vary slightly, so an exact total is less useful than the distinction between this early revival period and the subsequent standard East Indian rosewood production.

By late 1969, Martin was transitioning its rosewood models to East Indian rosewood. The factory D-45 of this period had non-scalloped bracing and square tube neck reinforcement; documented 1969 examples have a large rosewood bridge plate. Those features describe the late-1960s construction, independently of the exterior pearl work.

sections.heading: When Did The D-45 Change From Snowflakes To Hexagons?
sections.html: The standard D-45 inlay pattern changed to hexagons in 1939. The earlier snowflake pattern belongs to the first part of the original production run. The 2005 D-45 photograph used here is a later hexagon comparison, not a photograph of an original prewar guitar.

sections.heading: Was The 1968 D-45 Built Like A Prewar D-45?
sections.html: It restored the D-45 model and Style 45 appointments, but its non-scalloped bracing, square steel tube neck reinforcement and late-1960s bridge-plate specifications differed from prewar construction. Joe’s Martin construction timeline explains those changes across the broader guitar line.

title: Martin OM-18 History And Changes: 1930 To 1934
description: Original Martin OM-18 changes by year: the 1930 belly bridge, 1931 guards and tuners, 1932 dots, and the separate 1934 name and scale changes.
lede: The OM-18 began in 1930 as the mahogany-bodied Orchestra Model. During its short original run, Martin changed the bridge, enlarged the pickguard, replaced banjo-style tuners and extended the fingerboard markers. In 1934, the name changed to 000-18 before the scale became shorter.

hero.alt: Full front of a 2005 Martin OM-18GE shown as a modern comparison
hero.caption: 2005 Martin OM-18GE, a later recreation shown for body proportions. The guide below covers original prewar OM-18s.

sections.heading: OM-18 Changes By Year
sections.html:
Year Or PeriodWhat Changed
January 1930OM-18 production began, bringing mahogany back and sides to the long-scale, 14-fret Orchestra Model.
1930The belly bridge replaced the earliest straight bridge form.
1931A larger pickguard replaced the small teardrop guard. Open-back guitar tuners replaced the banjo-style machines in a separate transition during the year.
Early 1932Fingerboard dots extended beyond frets 5, 7 and 9 to include frets 12 and 15.
1934The model designation changed from OM-18 to 000-18. Early renamed guitars retained the long scale.
Later In 1934The 000-18 scale shortened from about 25.4 inches to 24.9 inches. T-frets and steel T-bar reinforcement also arrived in the successor era.

sections.heading: 1930: The Mahogany Orchestra Model
sections.html:
The first OM-18 shop order was placed in January 1930. The design combined a spruce top and mahogany back and sides with a 14-fret neck joint and approximately 25.4-inch scale. Its ebony fingerboard and bridge, simple dot markers and restrained trim distinguished Style 18 from the rosewood OM-28.

The Orchestra Model body was derived from the 000, with a shorter upper body to expose fourteen frets. The original OM-18 neck used bar frets and an ebony reinforcement strip. The later steel T-bar neck system had not yet entered production.

sections.heading: 1930: The Belly Bridge Replaces The Straight Bridge
sections.html:
The earliest OM-18 design used a plain straight bridge. During 1930, Martin adopted the belly bridge, widening the bridge behind the pin row. This was a change in the bridge’s footprint, not a change from mahogany to rosewood back and sides.

The bridge transition also affected the OM-28, whose earliest bridge had pyramid ends. Some earlier instruments still in factory stock received the new belly bridge before sale, so the original production sequence can include factory-updated guitars.

photos.alt: Wooden neck block of a modern Martin OM-18GE stamped Golden Era 1930 and serial 1055217
photos.caption: The 2005 OM-18GE's wooden neck block is stamped Golden Era and 1930 as the recreation reference; serial 1055217 dates the actual guitar to 2005.

sections.heading: 1931: Larger Pickguards And Guitar Tuners
sections.html:
The small teardrop pickguard gave way to a larger guard during 1931. Banjo-style tuners, with their mechanisms projecting behind the headstock, were also replaced by conventional open-back guitar tuners that year.

These were separate transitions. A larger guard did not necessarily arrive at exactly the same time as the newer tuner set. Later original OM-18s commonly combine the full-size guard with open-back Grover machines.

sections.heading: 1932 And 1933: The Longer Dot Pattern
sections.html:
Early Style 18 fingerboard markers occupied the fifth, seventh and ninth frets. In early 1932, the pattern extended to the twelfth and fifteenth frets. The additional markers are a dated decoration change within the original OM-18 run.

The OM-18 continued through 1933 with the long scale, 14-fret body and bar-fret neck construction. Its mahogany body remained the defining material difference from the OM-28.

sections.heading: 1934: The Name Changes Before The Scale
sections.html:
Martin changed the designation to 000-18 in 1934. The earliest guitars under the new name still had the long scale. Later that year, the scale shortened to approximately 24.9 inches.

T-shaped frets and steel T-bar neck reinforcement also entered production in 1934. Those changes belong to the successor 000 era. The Martin small-body guide follows the later 000 family.

sections.heading: Did All Original OM-18s Have Banjo Tuners?
sections.html: No. Banjo-style tuners belong to the earlier production, followed by conventional open-back guitar machines during 1931. Both types occur in the original OM-18 period.

sections.heading: Is An Early Long-Scale 000-18 An OM-18?
sections.html: It shares much of the preceding OM design, but Martin designated it 000-18. The 1934 name change and later scale change were separate events, so long scale alone does not supply the factory model name.

title: Martin OM-28 History And Specification Changes
description: Martin OM-28 development from 1929 through the 1969 revival: bridges, tuners, pickguards, fingerboard inlays and the 1934 move to the 000-28.
lede: The OM-28 introduced Martin’s long-scale, 14-fret Orchestra Model in 1929. Its original production evolved through bridge, guard, tuner and inlay changes before the model became the 000-28 in 1934. A six-guitar order revived the OM-28 name in 1969.

hero.alt: Full front of a 2005 Martin OM-28V shown as a modern comparison
hero.caption: 2005 Martin OM-28V, a later recreation shown for body proportions and herringbone trim. The guide covers the original OM-28 run and the 1969 revival.

sections.heading: OM-28 Changes By Year
sections.html:
Year Or PeriodWhat Changed
1929The first OM-28 developed from the 000-28 with a 14-fret neck joint and long scale.
1930The belly bridge replaced the early pyramid bridge.
1931Larger pickguards replaced the small teardrop form, and open-back guitar tuners replaced banjo-style machines in separate transitions.
Early 1932The diamonds-and-squares fingerboard pattern extended to the twelfth and fifteenth frets.
1934The model name changed to 000-28 while the earliest renamed guitars retained the long scale.
Later In 1934The 000-28 scale shortened to approximately 24.9 inches. T-frets and steel T-bar neck reinforcement replaced the earlier neck system during the successor era.
1969Eric Schoenberg’s six-guitar order revived the OM-28 through the Folklore Center and Matty Umanov.

sections.heading: 1929: The First Fourteen-Fret Orchestra Model
sections.html:
The OM-28 grew out of the 000-28 body family. Its shortened upper body and 14-fret neck joint increased access above the twelfth fret while retaining the approximately 25.4-inch scale. Brazilian rosewood back and sides, a spruce top, ebony fittings and herringbone top trim supplied the Style 28 specification.

The earliest custom guitar associated with Perry Bechtel had a requested 1 13/16-inch nut. That custom measurement should not replace the familiar 1 3/4-inch production OM specification. The beginning of the model includes development work as well as the settled production design.

sections.heading: 1930: From Pyramid To Belly Bridge
sections.html:
The first OM-28s had pyramid bridges. In 1930, the broader belly bridge replaced that form. The new bridge extended farther behind the pins while retaining ebony as the material.

Some unsold earlier guitars received belly bridges at the factory before shipment. The change therefore describes a production transition, not an exception-free rule tying one bridge outline to every guitar stamped during a particular month. The 2005 OM-28V photograph on this page illustrates the later belly outline, not an original 1930 instrument.

sections.heading: 1931: The Pickguard And Tuners Change Separately
sections.html:
The early small teardrop guard became a larger pickguard in 1931. Banjo-style tuners also gave way to conventional open-back guitar machines during the year.

The transitions overlapped. Larger-guard guitars can still have original banjo tuners, so the two features should not be described as a single simultaneous redesign. Both changes were established before the original OM-28 run ended.

sections.heading: 1932 And 1933: Fingerboard Decoration Extends Up The Neck
sections.html:
The early diamonds-and-squares pattern occupied the fifth, seventh and ninth frets. In early 1932, Style 28 added decoration at the twelfth and fifteenth frets.

The basic rosewood body, herringbone border, long scale and bar-fret neck continued through 1933. The original OM-28 used ebony neck reinforcement; the steel T-bar system arrived after the original OM production period.

sections.heading: 1934: The 000-28 Name And Shorter Scale
sections.html:
Martin renamed the model 000-28 in 1934. The first guitars carrying that name retained the long scale, and the reduction to roughly 24.9 inches followed later in the year.

The same successor period brought T-shaped frets and steel T-bar reinforcement. An early long-scale 000-28 can share dimensions with an OM-28 while carrying the later factory designation. The 0, 00 and 000 guide covers the continuing 000 history.

sections.heading: 1969: The OM-28 Revival
sections.html:
Eric Schoenberg ordered six OM-28s in 1969 through the Folklore Center and Matty Umanov. This revived the model decades after the original run.

The order belongs to a new production episode. It did not make every 1969 construction detail identical to a 1929 or 1933 OM-28. Original production and the revival should remain separate chapters of the model’s history.

sections.heading: When Did The Original OM-28 Run End?
sections.html: The original OM-28 period ended in 1933. In 1934, the successor carried the 000-28 name; the scale shortened later that year.

sections.heading: Did Every Original OM-28 Have A Pyramid Bridge?
sections.html: No. The pyramid bridge belongs to the earliest production. The belly bridge became the standard form during 1930 and remained through the rest of the original run.

title: Martin OM-45 And Deluxe History: 1930 To 1933
description: The original Martin OM-45 and Deluxe timeline: the 1930 introduction, Deluxe appointments, short Deluxe run and the end of OM-45 production in 1933.
lede: The OM-45 brought Style 45 pearl decoration to Martin’s long-scale, 14-fret Orchestra Model in 1930. The Deluxe was an additional trim version offered during the model’s first year. It disappeared before the standard OM-45, whose original run ended in 1933.

hero.alt: Full front of a 1976 Martin 000-45 used to compare Style 45 pearl ornament
hero.caption: 1976 Martin 000-45, shown as a later Style 45 ornament comparison. This is a 000-45; the guide below covers original prewar OM-45s.

sections.heading: Model Changes By Year
sections.html:
Year Or PeriodWhat Changed
1930The OM-45 introduced Style 45 pearl borders on the Orchestra Model body, with a long scale, 14-fret joint and Brazilian rosewood back and sides.
1930The Deluxe added an inlaid bridge and pickguard, plus engraved gold tuners with pearl buttons. It was a trim variant alongside the standard OM-45.
Within A YearThe Deluxe was discontinued within a year of its 1930 introduction. The standard OM-45 continued.
1933The original OM-45 run ended. Martin records 40 OM-45s built from 1930 through 1933.
1934Martin’s Orchestra Model naming gave way to 000, with neck and scale changes in the successor period. These changes occurred after the original OM-45 run.

sections.heading: 1930: Style 45 On The Orchestra Model Body
sections.html:
The OM-45 combined the 14-fret Orchestra Model outline and approximately 25.4-inch scale with Brazilian rosewood back and sides, a spruce top, and ebony fingerboard and bridge. Style 45 pearl borders extended around the top, back and sides.

The original neck used bar frets and ebony reinforcement. Those are construction features shared with the original OM period, separate from the additional ornament that distinguished the OM-45 from the OM-28.

photos.alt: Pearl back border and center strip on a 1976 Martin 000-45
photos.caption: Back-border pearl on the same 1976 000-45. This illustrates the location of Style 45 ornament, not the construction of a prewar OM-45.

sections.heading: 1930: The Deluxe Adds Inlaid Appointments
sections.html:
The Deluxe added pearl work to the bridge and pickguard and used engraved gold tuners with pearl buttons. Its solid headstock carried a torch inlay. The Deluxe was offered alongside the standard model; it was not a later replacement for all OM-45 production.

Photographs of surviving 1930 Deluxe instruments show small snowflake-style fingerboard ornament. That is an observation of those photographed guitars. The 1939 move to standard hexagons on the D-45 happened years after the original OM-45 run had ended.

sections.heading: The Deluxe Ends Before The Standard OM-45
sections.html:
The Deluxe was discontinued within a year of its 1930 introduction. Its elaborate appointments therefore belong to a short branch of the OM-45 story, rather than a feature set introduced across the whole line.

The standard OM-45 remained in production after the Deluxe disappeared. An inlaid guard added during a later repair does not represent a factory-wide change from standard OM-45 to Deluxe.

sections.heading: 1933: The Original OM-45 Run Ends
sections.html:
Martin records 40 OM-45s built between 1930 and 1933. The original production period ended in 1933, before the next year’s wider changes to model naming, scale length and neck construction.

Forty is the manufacturer’s recorded production count, not a count of surviving instruments. Later guitars and conversions using Style 45 decoration belong to separate production or repair histories.

sections.heading: 1934: Changes In The Successor Era
sections.html:
In 1934, Martin’s OM designation gave way to 000. The early renamed Orchestra Model guitars retained the long scale before the scale shortened later in the year. T-frets and steel T-bar reinforcement also arrived in 1934.

The original OM-45 had already left regular production when these changes arrived. The 1976 000-45 photograph on this page shows a later Style 45 instrument, rather than the construction of an original OM-45.

sections.heading: Did The Deluxe Replace The Standard OM-45?
sections.html: No. It was a more elaborate variant introduced in 1930, discontinued within a year. Standard OM-45 production continued through 1933.

sections.heading: Did Original OM-45s Use Steel T-Bar Neck Reinforcement?
sections.html: The original 1930 to 1933 OM production used ebony reinforcement and bar frets. Martin adopted steel T-bar reinforcement and T-shaped frets in 1934, after the original OM-45 run.

title: Early And Small Martin Guitars: Changes By Era
description: Early and small Martin development through 1969: body sizes, style numbers, mahogany and koa, steel strings, 14-fret models and the New Yorkers.
lede: Martin’s smaller guitars developed over more than a century, from early European-influenced designs to numbered sizes and styles, then to steel-string and 14-fret models. Changes followed different schedules for different sizes and styles. The dates below name the affected family instead of treating every small Martin as one model.
facts: Early Sizes, Small Bodies, Hawaiians And New Yorkers

hero.caption: An 1860s Martin 2½-17 in its coffin-style case, from the Joe's Vintage Guitars archive.

sections.heading: Model Changes By Year
sections.html:
Year Or PeriodWhat Changed
1830s To Mid-1800sEarly Stauffer-influenced construction gave way gradually to Spanish-influenced forms and the developing Martin body and bracing patterns.
1850s To 1902Style numbers and body sizes became more standardized. Size 0 appeared in the 1850s, 00 in the 1870s, and 000 in 1902.
1916Koa Hawaiian guitars supplied to Southern California Music Company established an early steel-string branch.
1917 And 1918Style 18 back and sides changed from rosewood to mahogany in 1917. Style 28 body binding changed from ivory to grained celluloid in 1918.
1922The all-mahogany 2-17 revived Style 17 as a standard Spanish-playing steel-string model.
1923 And 1926Steel strings became standard on Style 18 in 1923 and Style 28 in 1926. Special-order gut-string guitars remained possible.
1926 And 1929Style 18 moved from pyramid to plain rectangular bridges in 1926; Style 21 followed in 1929.
1932The 0-17 and 0-18 adopted 14-fret body forms. Other small models followed their own schedules.
1930s And 1940Small Style 18 models changed binding and fitting materials. Most settled on rosewood fingerboards and bridges in 1940 after earlier variation.
1961The 0-16NY and 00-21NY revived 12-fret, slotted-headstock forms with plain fingerboards and no pickguards.
1965 And 1966The usual steel-string saddle changed to a short drop-in form in 1965. Style 18 body binding changed to black Boltaron in 1966.

sections.heading: The 1800s: Designs Become Sizes And Styles
sections.html:
Early Martin guitars included Stauffer-style headstocks with tuners arranged on one side and adjustable-neck construction. Spanish-influenced designs and the developing Martin bracing system followed during an overlapping period of experimentation.

During the nineteenth century, repeatable body sizes and trim styles became more established. Style 28 used a herringbone top border; Style 26 used a half-herringbone border. Size 0 expanded the concert range in the 1850s, size 00 followed in the 1870s, and the larger 000 arrived in 1902. Earlier custom guitars do not always fit the later catalog combinations.

sections.heading: 1916 To 1926: Koa, Mahogany And Steel Strings
sections.html:
The koa Hawaiian guitars supplied in 1916 were an early steel-string branch. Their intended playing position and setup differed from ordinary Spanish-playing guitars. That development preceded the broader move to steel strings in the standard line.

Style 18 changed from rosewood to mahogany back and sides in 1917 while retaining a spruce top. In 1922, the all-mahogany 2-17 revived Style 17 as a steel-string model. Steel strings became standard on Style 18 in 1923 and Style 28 in 1926. Gut-string special orders continued, so the transition was not one date for every small Martin.

photos.alt: Engraved tuning-machine plate and three buttons on an 1860s Martin 2½-17
photos.caption: Engraved strip tuners on the 1860s 2½-17.

sections.heading: 1926 To 1934: Bridges And Neck Joints Change
sections.html:
Style 18 changed from pyramid bridges to plain rectangular bridges in 1926, and Style 21 followed in 1929. The belly bridge entered the Orchestra Model period in 1930. These are separate design steps, not different names for one bridge.

The 0-17 and 0-18 adopted 14-fret bodies in 1932. Their upper body outlines changed to provide the extra frets clear of the body. Other small models retained 12-fret configurations or changed on different schedules. Martin introduced T-shaped frets and steel T-bar neck reinforcement in its standard steel-string line in 1934; Hawaiian and special-order construction needs its own chronology.

sections.heading: The 1930s And 1940: Style 18 Materials Change
sections.html:
Style 18’s rosewood body binding gave way to black Fiberloid in 1934, followed by tortoise-colored plastic later in the decade. The exact sequence varied with body size.

Fingerboards and bridges also varied. Most smaller Style 18 guitars briefly used rosewood fittings in 1935, then returned chiefly to ebony before changing again to rosewood in 1940. The later D-18 material timetable should not be transferred to every 0, 00 and 000. The 0, 00 and 000 guide follows those families in more detail.

sections.heading: 1961: The New Yorker Models
sections.html:
The 0-16NY and 00-21NY returned to 12-fret neck joints and slotted headstocks. Both omitted the usual pickguard and front fingerboard markers. The 0-16NY used mahogany back and sides; the 00-21NY used rosewood.

These guitars retained X-bracing. Their plain appearance and slotted headstocks do not make them members of the fan-braced G and C classical families. The New Yorker designation describes a 1960s design program inspired by earlier Martins, not a nineteenth-century production date.

sections.heading: 1965 To 1969: Later Construction Changes
sections.html:
In 1965, the usual Martin steel-string bridge moved from the long through saddle to a short drop-in saddle. Style 18 binding changed from tortoise-colored material to black Boltaron in 1966.

Rosewood-bodied small guitars also reached Martin’s late-1969 transition toward East Indian rosewood. Those wood changes did not alter the distinction between size numbers and style numbers: the size identifies the body family, while the style identifies its appointment and material package.

sections.heading: Did All Small Martins Change To Steel Strings Together?
sections.html: No. Hawaiian steel-string instruments preceded the regular Spanish-playing steel-string line. The all-mahogany 2-17 appeared in 1922, Style 18 followed in 1923, and Style 28 in 1926. Special orders and earlier instruments require their own construction history.

sections.heading: When Did Martin Begin Using Serial Numbers?
sections.html: Martin’s regular guitar serial-number sequence began in 1898. Many earlier guitars therefore lack a modern-style serial. Model stamping became common later, around 1930. The serial and model-number guide explains those marking changes.

title: Martin Classical Guitars: G, C And N Changes
description: Martin classical guitar development from the 1936 G series to the 1962 C series and 1968 N series, with body, wood, scale and bracing changes.
lede: Martin’s dedicated classical line developed from the G series to the C and N families: G models from 1936, the C series from 1962, and the more Spanish-influenced N series from 1968. These families changed body shape and internal construction, while offering separate mahogany and rosewood versions.

hero.alt: Full front of a 1955 Martin 00-18G classical guitar
hero.caption: 1955 Martin 00-18G, showing its slotted headstock, 12-fret neck and tie-block bridge.

sections.heading: Model Changes By Year
sections.html:
Year Or PeriodWhat Changed
1936The G series established a dedicated gut-string line after the standard guitar range had moved toward steel strings.
1962The C series succeeded the G line. The 00-18C used the traditional elongated 12-fret 00 outline, and the 000-28C offered a larger rosewood body.
1966The rosewood 00-28C joined the range as a smaller companion to the 000-28C.
1968The N-10 and N-20 introduced a more Spanish-style classical body design.
1968 And 1969The early N-20 used a 25.4-inch scale, traditional Martin slotted headstock, seven fan braces and no bridge plate.
1969The 000-28C’s original run ended. The rosewood classical models reached Martin’s transition away from standard Brazilian rosewood production.

sections.heading: 1936: The G Series Restores A Dedicated Gut-String Line
sections.html:
After Martin’s standard Spanish-playing guitars moved toward steel strings in the 1920s, the G series supplied a separate gut-string design from 1936. Early experiments varied, so the familiar later G configuration should not be assigned unchanged to every first-year instrument.

The 00-18G used mahogany back and sides, while the 00-28G supplied rosewood. Both belonged to the lighter-string classical branch, with their own construction rather than the contemporary steel-string dreadnought timetable.

sections.heading: The Established G Body And Bracing
sections.html:
The later G design combined a 12-fret neck joint with the outline associated with the 14-fret 00 body. That combination placed the bridge differently from a traditional elongated 12-fret 00. A tie bridge secured the strings without the usual steel-string bridge pins.

The 00-28G bracing system used three fan struts and a mahogany bridge plate. These internal features distinguish the G design from the later N-20, whose seven-fan system omitted the bridge plate. The 1955 00-18G photographs here illustrate the established G-era string attachment.

photos.alt: Slotted headstock and large string rollers on a 1955 Martin 00-18G
photos.caption: The 1955 00-18G's slotted headstock and classical tuning machines.

sections.heading: 1962: The C Series Changes The Body Outline
sections.html:
The C series succeeded the G line in 1962. The mahogany 00-18C used the longer, traditional 12-fret 00 outline with fan bracing. The C designation accompanied this change to the body outline.

The rosewood 000-28C offered a larger body. Its production ran from 1962 through 1969. Size and style still mattered within the classical range: 00 and 000 identified different body families, while Style 18 and Style 28 separated the mahogany and rosewood versions.

sections.heading: 1966: The Rosewood 00-28C Joins The Range
sections.html:
The 00-28C added a smaller rosewood classical in 1966, with ebony fittings. It joined the 000-28C rather than immediately replacing it.

Both rosewood C body sizes therefore appear in the later 1960s. Their coexistence prevents a simple rule that every C-series rosewood Martin must be a 000 before 1966 and a 00 afterward.

sections.heading: 1968 And 1969: The N Series
sections.html:
The N-10 and N-20 arrived in 1968 with a more Spanish-influenced classical body. The N-10 used mahogany back and sides; the N-20 used rosewood. The early N-20 retained a 25.4-inch scale and Martin’s familiar slotted-headstock form.

Inside, the N-20 used seven fan braces and no bridge plate. That was a structural difference from the 00-28G’s three-strut and plate arrangement. Later N-series redesigns fall outside this guide’s 1969 endpoint.

Rosewood classical models also reached the late-1969 change toward East Indian rosewood. The G, C and N suffixes describe their design families; the wood species still depends on the production period and the actual instrument.

sections.heading: Did The C Series Begin In 1962 Or 1966?
sections.html: The C series began in 1962. The 1966 date belongs to the smaller rosewood 00-28C’s addition to the range. The larger 000-28C was already in production and continued through 1969.

sections.heading: Are The New Yorker Models Part Of The Classical Series?
sections.html: The 0-16NY and 00-21NY used 12-fret necks and slotted headstocks, but retained X-bracing. They belong to the small-body and New Yorker history, separate from the fan-braced G, C and N families.

title: Martin D12-20 And D12-35 History And Changes
description: Martin twelve-string changes through 1969: the D12-20 launch, the rosewood D12-35, 1967 pickguards, 1968 bridge plates and the rosewood transition.
lede: Martin’s regular twelve-string dreadnought line began with the D12-20 in late 1964, followed by the D12-35 in 1965. Both used a 12-fret body and short scale. Their first years brought pickguard and bridge-plate changes, while the D12-35 also reached the late-1969 rosewood transition.

hero.alt: Full front of a 1969 Martin D12-35 twelve-string guitar
hero.caption: 1969 Martin D12-35, showing the long slotted headstock and twelve-string bridge.

sections.heading: Model Changes By Year
sections.html:
Year Or PeriodWhat Changed
1921 And 1932A 1921 twelve-string 00-21 and a 1932 C-2 order were special projects, not a continuous catalog twelve-string line.
Late 1964The first D12-20 guitars were completed.
1965The D12-20 entered the catalog with a spruce top, mahogany back and sides, rosewood fittings, 12-fret neck and slotted headstock.
1965The D12-35 added a three-piece Brazilian rosewood back, bound ebony fingerboard and ebony bridge. Both models used a 24.9-inch scale and 1 7/8-inch nut.
1967 TransitionBlack pickguards replaced the earlier tortoise-pattern material, with transitional examples retaining the earlier guard.
1968Rosewood bridge plates began replacing maple, within Martin’s factory plate-material transition dated April 9, 1968.
Late 1969The D12-35 reached the change from Brazilian toward East Indian rosewood for standard back-and-side production.

sections.heading: Before 1964: Special Twelve-String Orders
sections.html:
Martin built occasional twelve-string instruments long before the D12 models. A purpose-built 00-21 was shipped in 1921, and an unusual C-2 archtop order followed in 1932.

Those isolated projects did not establish an uninterrupted twelve-string catalog family. The late-1964 D12-20 marks the beginning of the regular dreadnought program covered here.

sections.heading: Late 1964 And 1965: The D12-20
sections.html:
The first D12-20s were completed late in 1964 and appeared in the 1965 catalog. The design used a spruce top, mahogany back and sides, rosewood fingerboard and bridge, and a slotted headstock with six tuners on each side.

The neck joined the body at the twelfth fret. A 24.9-inch scale and 1 7/8-inch nut separated it from the usual long-scale, 14-fret six-string dreadnought. The bridge and headstock were laid out for twelve strings from the start.

photos.alt: Rear of a 1969 Martin D12-35 slotted headstock with twelve tuning buttons
photos.caption: The rear of the 1969 D12-35 headstock, with six tuning machines on each side.

sections.heading: 1965: The D12-35 Adds Rosewood And Style 35 Trim
sections.html:
The D12-35 joined the line in 1965. Its three-piece Brazilian rosewood back, bound ebony fingerboard and ebony bridge supplied a more elaborate alternative to the mahogany D12-20.

It retained the twelve-string family’s 12-fret neck joint, 24.9-inch scale and 1 7/8-inch nut. The three-piece back connected it visually to the six-string D-35, but the short scale and twelve-string layout made the D12-35 a separate design.

sections.heading: 1967: The Pickguard Transition
sections.html:
Early D12-20 and D12-35 guitars used tortoise-pattern pickguards. Black material entered during the 1967 transition.

This was a running production change. Some documented 1967 instruments retain the earlier tortoise-pattern guard, so 1967 should not be treated as a calendar boundary that makes every guitar identical. The mahogany-versus-rosewood distinction between the two models remained.

sections.heading: 1968 And 1969: Bridge Plates And Rosewood
sections.html:
Rosewood bridge plates began replacing the earlier maple plates in 1968. Martin’s broader factory change is dated April 9, 1968; a separate exact D12 serial cutoff is not established here. Plate material and plate dimensions are different specifications and need not have changed together.

The D12-35 reached the late-1969 shift toward East Indian rosewood for standard back-and-side production. The D12-20 remained the mahogany-bodied model. A 1969 serial does not, by itself, establish the species of a D12-35’s rosewood panels.

sections.heading: Did The D12-35 Have The Same Scale As The D-35?
sections.html: The original D12-35 used a 24.9-inch scale. The six-string D-35 used the longer 25.4-inch scale. Their shared Style 35 designation does not mean their neck and string layouts were the same.

sections.heading: Was 1965 The First Year Of The D12-20?
sections.html: It was the catalog introduction year. The first D12-20 instruments were completed in late 1964. The Martin serial-number chart dates production separately from the year a model appeared in a catalog.

title: Martin Tenor Guitar History And Model Changes
description: Martin tenor development from the 1927 size-5 models through the 1960s: 14-fret experiments, the 0-18T, belly bridges and Style 15 replacements.
lede: Martin’s tenor line began with small size-5 guitars in 1927. The next few years changed the body and neck relationship, leading to the 14-fret 0-18T and a better-placed bridge. Later additions brought all-mahogany bodies and simpler Style 15 versions.

hero.alt: Four-string 1927 Martin 5-21 tenor guitar in an open case
hero.caption: 1927 Martin 5-21 tenor guitar in its case.

sections.heading: Model Changes By Year
sections.html:
Year Or PeriodWhat Changed
1927The tenor family began with size-5 models, including the mahogany 5-17T and spruce-and-rosewood 5-21T.
1928The 2-18TL used a 14-fret neck on an earlier body outline, which placed the bridge high on the top.
Late 1929The Carl Fischer tenor shortened the upper body to expose fourteen frets while improving bridge placement.
1930The redesigned size-0 tenor entered the regular line as the 0-18T. Its upper bout became wider and flatter.
By 1931The 0-18T’s straight bridge gave way to a belly bridge.
1932The 0-17T added an all-mahogany option in the larger tenor body.
1949The 5-15T replaced the 5-17T with simpler Style 15 appointments and finish.
1960 To 1963The 0-15T offered the larger mahogany tenor with plain appointments and a satin finish.

sections.heading: 1927: The Size-Five Tenors
sections.html:
The early tenor line used Martin’s small size-5 body with four strings. The 5-17T had mahogany for the top, back and sides, while the 5-21T combined a spruce top with rosewood back and sides.

These models supplied guitar bodies for musicians moving from tenor banjo. The 1927 size-5 instrument shown here belongs to that first period. Scale lengths were not identical across every tenor model and later version, so a single measurement should not be assigned to the entire family.

sections.heading: 1928 And 1929: Fourteen-Fret Experiments
sections.html:
The 1928 2-18TL put a 14-fret neck on the earlier body outline. This moved the bridge high on the top. The design provided more frets clear of the body, but the resulting bridge position prompted a different body solution.

The late-1929 Carl Fischer tenor shortened the upper body instead. This preserved access to fourteen frets while allowing a more suitable bridge position. The change anticipated the shortened upper-body approach that became familiar on later Martin 14-fret guitars.

photos.alt: Upper body and herringbone rosette of a 1927 Martin 5-21 tenor
photos.caption: Four strings and the decorated rosette on the 1927 5-21 tenor.

sections.heading: 1930 And 1931: The Regular 0-18T
sections.html:
The redesigned tenor entered the regular Martin line as the 0-18T in 1930, following earlier development and examples recorded in 1929. Its upper bout became broader and flatter than the earlier form.

By 1931, a belly bridge had replaced the straight bridge on the 0-18T. The new body and the new bridge were distinct steps in the model’s development. The tenor line’s 14-fret history therefore begins before the general 1934 change often associated with Martin six-string models.

sections.heading: 1932: The All-Mahogany 0-17T
sections.html:
The 0-17T added a larger all-mahogany tenor in 1932. It offered a different material and decoration package from the spruce-topped 0-18T while using the size-0 tenor family.

The T suffix identifies the tenor branch. Body size and style still distinguish the models within it; 5-17T and 0-17T are not interchangeable names for the same guitar. The Martin model-number guide explains the size, style and suffix system.

sections.heading: 1949 To The 1960s: The Style 15 Models
sections.html:
The 5-15T replaced the 5-17T in 1949. It retained the small mahogany body while adopting the simpler Style 15 finish and appointments.

The larger 0-15T was produced from 1960 to 1963, also using mahogany with plain appointments and a satin finish. These were later model additions and replacements, not evidence that every earlier tenor received a new designation.

sections.heading: Did Martin Tenors Become Fourteen-Fret Guitars In 1934?
sections.html: The tenor line followed an earlier sequence: the 2-18TL experiment in 1928, the shortened Carl Fischer body in late 1929, and the regular 0-18T in 1930. The general six-string 1934 chronology does not describe that development.

sections.heading: Is A Plectrum Guitar The Same As A Tenor?
sections.html: Both can have four strings, but the plectrum design uses a longer neck and scale associated with plectrum-banjo playing. Martin’s plectrum models followed a separate, much shorter regular-production history.

description: Martin plectrum development from 1928 size-1 guitars to the 000 and OM forms, 1931 archtops, the end of regular production and later special orders.
lede: Martin’s plectrum guitars developed from small size-1 instruments into larger 000 and OM forms, then briefly into archtops. Regular production ended in 1931, although guitars remained on sale afterward and a few later special orders were built. Production dates and catalog dates are different parts of this history.

sections.heading: Model Changes By Year
sections.html:
Year Or PeriodWhat Changed
1928 And 1929Early plectrums used size-1 bodies and long four-string necks.
1930The larger 000-18P and 14-fret OM-18P broadened the plectrum range.
1931Martin built 65 OM-18Ps during the year and made small numbers of C-1 and C-2 archtop plectrums.
End Of 1931Regular plectrum production ended.
Through 1933The OM-18P remained offered for sale after the principal production period.
1940 And 1941Two plectrum special orders in 1940 and one in 1941 followed the discontinued regular line.

sections.heading: 1928 And 1929: The Small-Body Plectrums
sections.html:
The early plectrum family used a long four-string neck on a size-1 guitar body. Models such as the 1-17P and 1-28P combined that playing format with different style appointments.

The design addressed plectrum-banjo players. Its long scale separates it from the shorter tenor family, even though both have four strings. A later change in tuning does not represent a factory model change.

sections.heading: 1930: Larger 000 And OM Bodies
sections.html:
The 000-18P and OM-18P brought larger bodies to the plectrum line in 1930. The OM-18P used the 15-inch Orchestra Model body with fourteen frets clear, a spruce top, mahogany back and sides, and ebony fittings.

The P suffix kept the long-neck, four-string version distinct from the six-string OM-18. The larger body and 14-fret arrangement were changes in the factory design, while the four-string plectrum format remained.

sections.heading: 1931: The Last Main Production Year
sections.html:
Martin’s records show 65 OM-18Ps made in 1931. That is an annual total, not the lifetime total for the model: OM-18P production already existed in 1930.

Small numbers of C-1 and C-2 archtop plectrums also appeared in 1931. These extended the plectrum format into Martin’s new archtop body family, with an arched top and floating bridge arrangement rather than the OM flat-top construction.

sections.heading: 1932 And 1933: Sales Continue After Production Stops
sections.html:
Regular plectrum production ended in 1931. The OM-18P nevertheless remained offered for sale through 1933.

A later price-list appearance does not establish a new production batch. This distinction explains why the sales history extends beyond the main manufacturing period without requiring a new model specification for each listed year.

sections.heading: 1940 And 1941: Isolated Special Orders
sections.html:
Two plectrum orders followed in 1940, with another in 1941. These were exceptions after the regular line had ended, rather than a sustained revival of the plectrum range.

Later six-string conversions of plectrum guitars belong to individual repair histories. They do not change the original model’s production dates or demonstrate that Martin introduced a six-string replacement under the P designation.

sections.heading: Were All OM-18Ps Built In 1931?
sections.html: No. Martin’s plectrum records include OM-18P production in 1930 as well as 1931. The often-quoted 65 instruments is the 1931 total.

sections.heading: Does A 1933 Catalog Listing Mean A 1933 Guitar?
sections.html: No. OM-18Ps remained offered after regular plectrum production ended in 1931. The serial-number guide dates the guitar separately from a catalog or purchase date.

title: Martin Archtop History: C, R And F Model Changes
description: Martin acoustic archtop changes from 1931 to 1942: round holes and f-holes, pressed and carved tops, larger F bodies and the final production batches.
lede: Martin’s acoustic archtops developed through three parallel families between 1931 and 1942. The C models began with carved tops and round soundholes; the smaller R series used pressed tops before the R-18 changed construction; and the F series introduced a wider 16-inch body. Soundholes, top construction and body size changed on separate schedules.

hero.alt: Full front of a sunburst 1934 Martin C-2 archtop
hero.caption: 1934 Martin C-2 archtop, showing its f-holes, floating bridge and tailpiece.

sections.heading: Model Changes By Year
sections.html:
Year Or PeriodWhat Changed
1931The C series began with 15-inch bodies, carved spruce tops and round soundholes. C-1 used mahogany; C-2 and C-3 used rosewood with increasingly elaborate trim.
1932 To 1933F-holes replaced the early round-hole C design. The smaller R-18 appeared with a pressed spruce top and also moved from a round soundhole to f-holes.
December 1934The R-17 added a mahogany-topped version to the smaller archtop family.
1935The F-7 and F-9 introduced wider 16-inch archtop bodies.
Mid-1936The R-18 changed from a pressed top with segmented f-holes to a carved top with continuous f-holes.
1940The simpler F-1 and F-2 joined the 16-inch range, with mahogany and rosewood back and sides respectively.
1942Final C production came in August, the last F batch in September, and the final R-18 batch in November.

sections.heading: 1931: The Round-Hole C Series
sections.html:
The first C-series batch dates to June 1931. The guitars had 15-inch bodies, carved spruce tops and round soundholes. C-1 used mahogany back and sides, while C-2 and C-3 used rosewood, with the C-3 receiving more elaborate decoration.

The raised top carried a floating bridge and tailpiece. Martin’s archtop construction should not be equated with a carved back: the company also shaped thin back plates with internal braces. Top arching and back construction are separate specifications.

sections.heading: 1932 And 1933: F-Holes And The Smaller R-18
sections.html:
During 1932 and 1933, f-holes replaced the earliest round-hole C design. The transition was not one simultaneous change across every model.

The smaller R-18 began with a pressed spruce top. Its early round-soundhole form also gave way to f-holes. Pressing a thin plate into an arch and carving an arch from thicker wood are different construction methods, even when the resulting guitars share a similar outline.

sections.heading: 1934 And 1935: The R-17 And Wider F Models
sections.html:
The R-17 arrived in December 1934 with a mahogany top. It provided a different material option within the smaller archtop family.

In 1935, the F-7 and F-9 expanded Martin’s archtop body width to 16 inches. These larger models occupied a more elaborate tier above the smaller guitars. Their acoustic F designation is separate from the F-series electrics introduced decades later.

sections.heading: Mid-1936: The R-18 Adopts A Carved Top
sections.html:
The R-18 changed from a pressed top to a carved top in mid-1936. The earlier segmented f-holes gave way to continuous f-hole openings with the revised construction.

This is a dated structural change within one model. A rule that every R-18 had a pressed top would miss the later version, while a rule that every Martin archtop was carved would miss the earlier R-18.

sections.heading: 1940 To 1942: Simpler F Models And The End Of Production
sections.html:
The F-1 and F-2 joined the 16-inch family in 1940 with simpler decoration. The F-1 used mahogany back and sides; the F-2 used rosewood. Total acoustic F-series production was 401 guitars, including 91 F-1s.

The original acoustic archtop line ended in 1942. The final C guitars were made in August, the final F batch in September, and the last R-18 batch in November. Later flat-top conversions of these bodies are individual modifications, not a further factory archtop model period.

sections.heading: Did Martin Archtops Always Have F-Holes?
sections.html: No. The first C-series guitars had round soundholes, and the early R-18 also used a round soundhole. F-holes entered during the early-1930s development of the line.

sections.heading: Were All R-18 Tops Pressed?
sections.html: No. Earlier R-18 tops were pressed, but the model changed to a carved top in mid-1936. The change also replaced the segmented f-hole arrangement with continuous openings.

title: Martin Electric Guitar History: E, F And GT Changes
description: Martin electric changes from 1959 through 1968: electrified flat-tops, F-series hollowbodies, the GT redesign, twelve strings and production endings.
lede: Martin’s early electric history moved through three designs: flat-top acoustics fitted with pickups, the thin hollowbody F series, and the redesigned GT series. The changes involved body shape, pickup layout, bridge construction and neck design. Catalog availability sometimes continued after production ended.

hero.alt: Full front of a cherry Martin GT-75 electric guitar with two pickups and vibrato tailpiece
hero.caption: Martin GT-75 from the Joe's Vintage Guitars archive, showing the double-cutaway body and two-pickup layout.

sections.heading: Model Changes By Year
sections.html:
Year Or PeriodWhat Changed
1959The 00-18E joined the electrified flat-top range with a DeArmond pickup and top-mounted controls; a second pickup was available.
1961F-50, F-55 and F-65 prototypes introduced thin hollowbody designs. The F-50 had one pickup, the F-55 two, and the F-65 added a second cutaway.
1962The F series moved into larger production with an adjustable clear plexiglass bridge.
196400-18E production ended, although remaining guitars were still listed the following year.
1965F-series production ended as the GT-70 and GT-75 arrived with a revised body and neck design.
1966GT-70 production ended after the 1965 and 1966 run.
1967A twelve-string GT-75 appeared briefly. GT-series production ended that year.
1968GT models still appeared in catalogs and price lists after manufacturing had stopped.

sections.heading: 1959: The Electrified Flat-Tops
sections.html:
The 00-18E retained a flat-top acoustic body while adding a DeArmond pickup and controls on the top. A second pickup was available. The model belonged to the same early electric effort as the larger D-18E and D-28E.

This first approach adapted the acoustic platform. The later F series was a different thin hollowbody design, so the shift was more substantial than adding another pickup to the 00-18E.

sections.heading: 1961 And 1962: The F-Series Hollowbodies
sections.html:
The first F-50, F-55 and F-65 prototypes and small batches date to 1961, followed by larger production in 1962. The F-50 used one pickup. The F-55 added a second pickup, and the F-65 used the two-pickup arrangement with a double-cutaway body.

An adjustable clear plexiglass bridge was part of the original F-series design. A later wood or metal replacement on an individual guitar is not a new factory model phase. The F model numbers distinguished simultaneous versions, rather than a sequence in which every F-50 became an F-55 and then an F-65.

photos.alt: Sunburst single-cutaway Martin F-series electric with two pickups and a V-shaped tailpiece
photos.caption: A Martin F-series electric from the JVG archive, shown for comparison with the GT-75's different body and headstock shapes. Exact year is not recorded with this photo.

sections.heading: 1964 And 1965: The Early Electric Lines End
sections.html:
00-18E production ended in 1964, but the model remained in the next year’s price list while stock was available. The F series ended in 1965.

Martin built 519 F-50s in total, with only one recorded in the final year. These production dates explain why a sales listing or catalog date may be later than the manufacturing period.

sections.heading: 1965 And 1966: The GT Redesign
sections.html:
The GT-70 and GT-75 arrived in 1965 with a revised body, bolt-on neck construction and an adjustable neck rod. GT-70 identified the single-cutaway version; GT-75 identified the double-cutaway version. A Bigsby vibrato was optional.

The GT hardware and neck arrangement differed from the earlier flat-top electrics. GT-70 production lasted through 1966, while the GT-75 continued into the following year. Headstock outlines and finishes varied within the GT period and should not be turned into unsupported one-year cutoffs.

sections.heading: 1967 And 1968: Twelve Strings And Remaining Stock
sections.html:
A twelve-string GT-75 appeared briefly in 1967. Its elongated conventional headstock accommodated twelve tuners, setting it apart from the six-string GT headstock forms.

GT-series production ended in 1967. Catalog and price-list appearances continued in 1968, reflecting continued availability rather than another year of manufacture. The twelve-string version was a short addition at the end of the line.

sections.heading: Was The F Series A Continuation Of Martin’s Acoustic F Archtops?
sections.html: No. The acoustic F-1, F-2, F-7 and F-9 belonged to the 1930s and 1940s archtop family. The F-50, F-55 and F-65 were thin hollowbody electrics introduced in 1961.

sections.heading: Were GT Guitars Still Being Made In 1968?
sections.html: GT production ended in 1967. The models remained in 1968 catalogs and price lists, so a later advertisement does not establish a 1968 build date.
